key_terms.meaning: The bit field of an instruction that names the operation to be done, for example the 8 bits 0011 1010 mean MOV A,M on the 8085.
The data an instruction works on, given as a register name, an immediate value, or a memory address.
The fixed way the bits of an instruction are split into opcode and operand/address fields, such as 4-bit opcode + 12-bit address.
The rule the CPU follows to work out the effective address of an operand from the bits given in the instruction.
The final memory address the CPU actually reads or writes after the addressing rule is applied.
The operand value is carried inside the instruction itself, e.g. MOV A,#32H loads the number 32H.
The instruction names a register that holds the address, e.g. MOV A,@R0 reads the byte pointed to by R0.
Effective address = base register + index register + displacement, used for arrays and look-up tables.
An instruction that only copies a byte or word between registers, memory, ports or the stack, e.g. MOV, PUSH, IN, OUT.
A set of single bits (carry, zero, sign, parity, auxiliary carry, overflow) set by the ALU after an operation and tested later by branches.
Set to 1 when an addition produces a carry out of the top bit, or a subtraction needs a borrow.
Subtracts the operand from a register only to set flags; neither the register nor the operand is changed.
A jump that changes the program counter only if a named flag has a stated value, e.g. JZ jumps when zero flag = 1.
Pushes the address of the next instruction on the stack, then loads the program counter with the subroutine address.
A register that holds the address of the top of the stack; PUSH decrements and POP increments it on the 8051.
Last in, first out: the item pushed last is the item popped first, which is why nested calls return in the right order.
The time one basic CPU operation takes; on the 8051 one machine cycle = 12 clock cycles = 1 µs at 12 MHz.
A block of constants in program memory that a program reads with an index instead of computing the value.
A program that translates assembly source text into machine code and resolves labels to addresses.
Software that runs the machine code instruction by instruction on a PC, showing registers, memory and flags without any hardware.

takeaways: Every instruction is bits split into an opcode and operand fields, so the CPU decodes the opcode first and the operand second.
The addressing mode decides where the operand lives; the same opcode with a different mode can mean register, memory, or an immediate value.
Data transfer instructions move bytes but never touch the flags, which is why MOV is safe between a CMP and a conditional jump.
Arithmetic and logical instructions leave their result in flags, and every conditional branch is really a test of one of those flags.
JMP changes the program counter and never comes back; CALL saves a return address on the stack so RET can come back.
The stack is LIFO memory, so pushing the registers at the start of a subroutine and popping them before RET keeps the caller's data safe.
A delay loop's time is found by multiplying the loop count by the machine cycles per iteration and the machine cycle time.
A look-up table trades memory for speed: seven-segment codes, sine values and square-wave patterns are read by index, not calculated.
The assembler turns text into machine code, the simulator runs that code with no chip, and an IDE wraps both with an editor and a debugger.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always pair theory with a program: the examiner wants the definition and format drawn out, then a working assembly listing with the register, flag and stack effects traced line by line.

bank.q: Define an instruction format. Draw the field split of a 16-bit instruction carrying a 4-bit opcode and a 12-bit address, and classify instruction sets by the function each group performs.
outline: Definition of instruction as a coded command
Opcode field vs operand/address field with bit counts shown
Diagram of the 16-bit split
Functional classes: data transfer, arithmetic, logical, branch/control, machine control
One example instruction named for each class

bank.q: Explain any six addressing modes with a one-line example of each, and state which mode suits array handling and why.
outline: Definition of addressing mode and effective address
Immediate, direct, register, register indirect, indexed, implied/implied-register
One example instruction per mode with the effective address worked out
Indexed mode fits arrays because base + index walks through consecutive bytes
Note that the same opcode can pair with several modes

bank.q: Explain the flag register of an 8-bit microprocessor. Describe how the zero, carry and sign flags are set, and how a conditional jump uses them.
outline: List of flags and the bit each occupies
Carry set by carry-out or borrow; zero set when result is 00H; sign copies the top bit
Example: CMP then JZ
Flags are not changed by MOV, only by ALU operations
Why the branch must follow the flag-setting instruction immediately

bank.q: Classify data transfer instructions and explain with examples the difference between MOV, XCHG, PUSH/POP and IN/OUT.
outline: Meaning of data transfer and the fact that flags are not affected
MOV between register, memory and immediate
XCHG as an exchange, not a copy
PUSH/POP using the stack pointer
IN/OUT for ports with the port address
Size and cycle differences

bank.q: Write an assembly program to add two 16-bit numbers stored in memory locations 2000H and 2002H and store the 16-bit sum at 2004H, keeping the carry.
outline: Load low bytes and add with ADD/ADD
Add high bytes with ADC to take in the carry
Store low byte then high byte
Show the register allocation table
State the effect on carry and zero flags
Comment every line

bank.q: Write an assembly program to find the largest byte in a block of N bytes starting at a given address, and draw the flowchart.
outline: Counter in one register, pointer in another
Compare using CMP or a subtract that sets flags
Conditional jump to skip the update when the candidate is smaller
Decrement counter with DJNZ or DEC+JNZ
Flowchart with the decision diamond
Final result stored in a named memory location

bank.q: Write a delay routine that produces a 1 ms delay on a microcontroller running from a 12 MHz crystal. Show the machine cycle count.
outline: 1 machine cycle = 12 clock cycles = 1 µs at 12 MHz
DJNZ takes 2 machine cycles = 2 µs
Loop count = 500 µs from DJNZ alone; add MOV and loop overhead
Two nested loops or a count of 250 with a 2 µs body
Show the arithmetic step by step with units
State that the delay is approximate and depends on crystal tolerance

bank.q: Write a program that reads the numbers 0 to 9 from a look-up table and sends the matching seven-segment code to a port.
outline: Table of segment codes stored with DB/DT directive
Base address of the table in a register pair
Index added to base with indexed addressing
MOVC or equivalent table-read instruction
Code sent to the output port
Table saved in program memory, not RAM

bank.q: Compare the JMP and CALL instructions. Trace the contents of the stack, the stack pointer and the program counter when a CALL is executed and RET returns.
outline: JMP loads PC only; CALL loads PC and saves the return address
Stack grows downward so SP is decremented on PUSH
Low byte then high byte pushed on the 8051
RET pops high byte then low byte back into PC
Numeric trace of SP before and after each step
Nested calls and why the order is LIFO

bank.q: Explain the stack and subroutine mechanism in detail. Show how a subroutine that uses four registers is protected, and what happens if the registers are not saved.
outline: Stack definition, LIFO, SP as top-of-stack pointer
CALL pushes return address; RET pops it
PUSH of the four registers at entry and POP in reverse order at exit
Order of POP must be the reverse of PUSH
If registers are not saved the caller's values are corrupted
Nesting depth limited by available stack RAM

bank.q: Write a subroutine that multiplies two 8-bit numbers by repeated shift-and-add, and a main program that calls it twice with different inputs.
outline: Product register cleared, multiplier and multiplicand loaded
Shift right the multiplier, test the carry
Add multiplicand to a 16-bit partial product when the bit is 1
Shift the multiplicand left
DJNZ loop and RET at the end
Main program calls the subroutine twice and shows the return address handling

bank.q: Distinguish between an assembler, a cross-assembler, a linker, a simulator and an IDE, and explain the order in which they are used to build and test a program.
outline: Assembler: source text to object code, resolves labels, handles directives
Cross-assembler runs on a PC but produces code for another chip
Linker joins object modules and fixes addresses
Simulator executes the object code and shows registers, memory and flags
IDE puts editor, assembler, downloader and debugger in one window
Order: edit, assemble, link, simulate or download, debug

bank.q: A given assembly routine reads a keypad, ignores contact bounce with a delay loop, and converts the key number with a look-up table. Analyse the routine line by line, state the total delay, and say which registers it destroys.
outline: Identify the input port read and how a key is detected
Count the delay loop cycles and convert to microseconds
Explain the look-up table indexing and its stored codes
List every register written and whether it is saved
Suggest protect/restore with PUSH and POP
Comment on one bug such as missing debounce on release

bank.q: Compare a table-driven seven-segment display routine with a routine that computes the segment code by logic, on the basis of memory used, execution time and ease of modification.
outline: Table method: constants in program memory, one indexed read, easy to edit
Computed method: bit tests or arithmetic, fewer bytes, more cycles and more code
Memory vs time trade-off stated in numbers
Table wins for irregular patterns, computation wins for sequential codes
Effect on maintainability
Recommendation with reason

glossary.def: A coded command held in memory that tells the CPU one basic operation and the data it works on.
The bits of an instruction that identify the operation.
The data or the address of the data on which an instruction acts.
The complete list of instructions a processor can decode and execute.
The rule that converts the address field of an instruction into the effective address of the operand.
The memory address finally used for the read or write.
A constant carried inside the instruction, written with a # sign in many assemblers.
A mode where the instruction holds the full memory address of the operand.
A mode where the instruction holds an address, and that address holds the address of the operand.
A mode where a named register holds the address of the operand.
A register whose contents are added to a base address to step through a table or array.
A single bit set or cleared by the ALU to record some property of the last result.
A flag set by a carry from bit 3 to bit 4, used by decimal-adjust instructions.
The way negative numbers are stored: invert all bits and add one.
An instruction that shifts bits left or right and moves the bit pushed out into the carry flag.
The register holding the address of the next instruction to be fetched.
A jump that takes place only if a stated flag value is present.
A named block of code that the main program can call again and again and which returns when finished.
Calling a subroutine from inside another subroutine, which uses extra stack space.
A LIFO area of memory used for return addresses and saved register values.
The time the CPU takes for one basic bus operation; on the 8051 it is 12 clock cycles.
One clock period of the processor; a machine cycle contains a fixed number of T-states.
A list of pre-computed constants read by an index instead of being calculated at run time.
A line in assembly source that tells the assembler what to do, such as ORG or DB, and does not become a machine instruction.
An assembler that runs on one computer but produces machine code for a different processor.
The intermediate file of machine code and relocation information produced by the assembler.
A tool that lets you run code one instruction at a time and inspect registers and memory.
